To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CEOs who are greedy and are paid with a high proportion of equity are less likely to invest in CSR and that these firms will experience higher stock losses in the short-run and take longer time to fully recover from the 2018 GFC than firms led by non-greedy CEOs.
CEO greed is negatively associated with CSR investment, and CSR investment is positively related to firm performance.

CEOs' greed is negatively related to CSR and that this relationship is more negative for CEOs who receive more stock based compensation and more positive for CEOs who receive less stock based compensation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of CEO greed in the context of corporate social responsibility and its impact on firm resilience.
CEO greed and how this relates to CSR and the ability of organizations to recover from systemic shocks.
the impact of CEO greed on CSR and the implications for firm resilience during systemic shocks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our results suggest that CEO greed is associated with low investment in CSR which is, in turn, related to poor organizational outcomes during and after the 2008 financial crisis.
the CEO greed is a negative predictor for corporate social responsibility, which in turn, is a negative predictor of the firm’s performance in the short run.
the results of this study suggest that the pursuit of personal wealth by CEOs is associated with lower CSR investments and lower resilience in the wake of systemic shocks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the greed of CEOs has negative consequences for multiple stakeholders and the long run performance of the organization.
greedy CEOs, in the absence of a strong pay-for-performance incentive, will tend to neglect investment in CSR, which, in turn, will lead to greater losses in the aftermath of a systemic shock.
greedy CEOs are more concerned about personal wealth than about long term stakeholder interests, which may have negative implications for the well being of their firms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pursuit of personal wealth by CEOs may have long run consequences for firms and stakeholders.
CEO greed can have a long-term negative impact on the firm's performance.
, in the face of systemic shocks, greedy CEOs are likely to be less concerned about the well being of their organizations and stakeholders, which may result in lower organizational resilience.
